plan.scope: Only new-block batching; format, logical block size, checkpoint parameters, durability and transaction boundaries unchanged. No comparison service is started.

fuse.order: before/after then after/before, each three times
fuse.validation: full SHA-256 readback, quick_check, unmount timing

plan.prohibition: No owned builds or tests during measurement
plan.retention: keep every sample, errors, logs, code/binary hashes and cleanup manifests; remove owned DBs after shutdown outside timers

tmpfs.scope: Instrumented native 256 MiB write+fsync with split FUSE-size requests. tmpfs isolates SQL/CPU costs and is not a physical durability benchmark.

ext4.scope: Instrumented native 256 MiB write+fsync with split FUSE-size requests. tmpfs isolates SQL/CPU costs and is not a physical durability benchmark.

config.fuse: live direct_io with writeback disabled; unchanged production mount adapter

interpretation: The tmpfs result isolates reduced SQL and block-processing work; it is not a physical durability measurement.
The query/batch optimization leaves payload layout, WAL volume, request commits and checkpoint budget unchanged.
All physical-disk samples are retained; SQLite sync/checkpoint I/O still causes long stalls. Do not attribute every median difference to the SQL change.

Fault-injection tests initially mixed Python SQLite 3.45.1 and the private SQLite 3.53.2 in one process. The same failure reproduces on baseline. Both raw inspection and DDL now run in a subprocess; native fault tests use the single bundled SQLite. See https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html#multiple_copies_of_sqlite_linked_into_the_same_application
